records.issue_text: [BUG] ProvideAnonDBStore's signature gains a new `deviceLimit int64` parameter, but every other registration/call site of this provider outside this diff (fx/wire registration of the anon store) is not updated, leaving a DI graph that can no longer supply the new int64 argument. Grafana constructs providers via fx; a ProvideAnonDBStore registered through fx.Provide now requires an int64 that the container does not provide (the value lives inside *setting.Cfg, not as a standalone int64), so the server fails at startup with a dependency-injection error even though impl.go builds its own instance manually.

records.issue_text: [BUG] updateDevice passes the SQL query string as args[0] to dbSession.Exec, i.e. `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)` then `dbSession.Exec(args...)`, relying on sqlx-style Exec(sqlOrArgs...) accepting the query as the first variadic element; with the sqlstore DBSession wrapper this dispatches the query as a bound parameter rather than a statement. If DBSession.Exec does not treat the first variadic element as the query, every device-limit-exceeded update fails with a SQL syntax/bind error, and CreateOrUpdateDevice returns a raw SQL error instead of ErrDeviceLimitReached, so anonymous authentication breaks whenever the configured limit is hit.

records.issue_text: [BUG] The device limit is enforced with a check-then-act pattern: a SELECT COUNT followed by a separate insert/update, with no unique constraint or transactional guard, so the limit is racy. N concurrent anonymous authentication requests all read count < deviceLimit and all insert, overshooting the configured limit by up to N-1 devices per race window; the limit is a soft suggestion, not an invariant.
records.rationale: In `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, the limit check does `CountDevices(...)` and then, if `count < s.deviceLimit`, proceeds to the normal insert/upsert path as a separate operation (`count, err := s.CountDevices(...)` then later executes DB write). There is no transactional/locking guard tying the count to the subsequent insert/update, so concurrent requests can all observe `count < limit` and each insert a new device, overshooting the limit. The diff shows no DB constraint or atomic update that would enforce the limit under concurrency.

records.issue_text: [BUG] TagDevice now returns errors from tagDeviceUI (previously only logged at Debug and returned nil), which combined with client.go's propagation turns any transient DB error during device tagging into a failed anonymous authentication. A transient database error on the anon_device table (previously tolerated by design — logged, auth proceeded) now returns 500s to every anonymous user, changing the accepted failure contract of anonymous auth.
records.rationale: The diff does change `TagDevice` to return the error from `tagDeviceUI` (`impl.go`: added `return err` after logging), but it does NOT make “any transient DB error” fail anonymous authentication. In `client.go`, the new synchronous call only propagates (returns) the error when `errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached) { return nil, err }`; for all other errors it just logs a warning and continues to return an anonymous identity. This contradicts the finding’s claim that transient DB errors now cause failed auth/500s for anonymous users.

Operators who set device_limit as a resource/cost control see it silently violated under concurrent load (N concurrent anonymous requests all read count below the limit and all insert), and since the limit now also gates authentication, the same race makes the enforcement guarantee unenforceable as a security boundary.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] updateDevice lets an unauthenticated caller overwrite the client_ip and user_agent of any existing device row within the expiry window, keyed solely on the client-supplied device_id with no ownership or verification check. Once the limit is reached, any anonymous request whose derived device_id collides with an existing active device rewrites that device's recorded IP/UA, so an attacker can poison the audit/telemetry records of other anonymous users; combined with the count race above, the update path also becomes the only write path, making the poisoning reliable.

records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The device-limit check is a check-then-act race: CountDevices is read outside any transaction with the subsequent insert, so concurrent anonymous requests can all observe count < deviceLimit and insert, exceeding the configured limit. Operators setting device_limit get a soft limit that overshoots under bursty anonymous traffic; there is no unique constraint or atomic guard enforcing the cap, and the overshoot is silent (no log when it happens).
